subsystems.name: Electrode array
subsystems.role: the part in contact with neurons — a flexible mesh or stent-mounted film that records and stimulates.
parts: conductive polymer or thin-film metal traces

subsystems.name: Delivery system
subsystems.role: gets the array into the brain without open surgery on the cortex.
parts: fine needle or syringe for tissue injection
catheter and guidewire for endovascular routes
deployment mechanism that unfurls the mesh or expands the stent

subsystems.name: On-implant electronics
subsystems.role: amplifies and digitises faint neural signals next to the source.

subsystems.name: Wireless link and power
subsystems.role: carries data and power through skin and bone with no wires crossing the body.

subsystems.name: External unit and decoding
subsystems.role: turns spike trains into commands and streams feedback back.

subsystems.name: Biocompatibility barrier
subsystems.role: keeps the immune system from walling off the electrodes.

buildSteps.title: Design the electrode map
buildSteps.detail: Decide how many channels are needed, how densely they must sit, and which brain regions they must reach.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the mesh
buildSteps.detail: Thin polymer and metal layers are patterned on a sacrificial wafer by the same lithography used for computer chips, then released as a free-standing, flexible mesh with conducting pathways and recording sites.

buildSteps.title: Mount or compress it
buildSteps.detail: For an endovascular device, electrodes are fixed onto a self-expanding metal stent. For an injectable mesh, the whole structure is folded and drawn into the bore of a needle of roughly 100 micrometres.

buildSteps.title: Add the chip
buildSteps.detail: A low-power amplifier and multiplexer is bonded to the array's tail so raw signals leave the body already digitised.

buildSteps.title: Coat for the body
buildSteps.detail: Antifouling and anti-inflammatory coatings are applied to reduce the scar tissue that otherwise insulates electrodes.

buildSteps.title: Deliver it
buildSteps.detail: Either inject through a small opening in the skull into the cortex, letting the mesh unfurl among neurons, or thread a catheter through a neck vein into a large blood vessel lying against the brain surface, where the stent opens against the vessel wall.

buildSteps.title: Link and calibrate
buildSteps.detail: The external unit pairs with the implant, checks electrode impedance and records baseline activity.

buildSteps.title: Close the loop
buildSteps.detail: Decoding software learns the person's neural patterns, and stimulation channels return information — the step that would make this a two-way interface.

prerequisites.why: mesh and polymer arrays have been made and implanted in animals, proving the fabrication route works.
stent-mounted electrode arrays have been implanted in human clinical trials, but channel counts and longevity are limited.

prerequisites.tech: Low-power implantable chips and wireless links
prerequisites.why: hearing implants and deep-brain stimulators already run for years inside the body.
scar tissue and corrosion degrade recordings within months to a few years; a lifelong interface needs far longer.
current systems read a few hundred channels for cursor or speech control; 'seamless, high-speed' links need orders of magnitude more.

pathway.milestone: endovascular electrode arrays in human trials restoring typing and communication for people with paralysis; injectable mesh electrodes shown in animals
pathway.unlocks: proof that a brain interface can be installed without opening the skull.

pathway.milestone: wireless mesh implants with several hundred to a few thousand stable channels
pathway.unlocks: richer signals for speech and prosthetic control, without a cable through the skin.

pathway.milestone: bidirectional implants that write as well as read, with decade-scale stability
a distributed, body-wide mesh linking brain to digital systems at high bandwidth
pathway.unlocks: the 'neural lace' idea proper — still speculative, and gated by biology more than by electronics.
